sections.s07.s0: Work from pixels up: arrays and classical OpenCV operations first (s0.0 to s0.2), then CNNs, transfer learning and augmentation (s0.3 to s0.5), then detection metrics, evaluation and video (s0.6 to s0.8). Spend at least half the time running code on your own images rather than reading.
sections.s07.s1: Fix the task and dataset first, since every later step depends on them. Train a baseline before fine-tuning, keep the test split untouched until the metrics step, and build the inference command last.

s07.s0.0.how: Load an image with cv2.imread and print its shape and dtype. Convert BGR to RGB and HSV with cv2.cvtColor, split the channels, and compare adding two uint8 images with + against cv2.add.
s07.s0.0.done: You can explain why OpenCV loads BGR, why 200 + 100 gives 44 in uint8, and how to convert an image to float in [0, 1].

s07.s0.1.how: On one noisy photo apply GaussianBlur, then threshold with Otsu, then Canny, then morphologyEx with opening and closing. Change one parameter at a time and save each output side by side.
s07.s0.1.done: You can clean speckle noise and small holes from a binary mask and explain what each kernel size changed.

s07.s0.2.how: Detect ORB keypoints in two photos of the same flat object, match them with BFMatcher, estimate a homography with cv2.findHomography using RANSAC, and warp one image onto the other with warpPerspective.
s07.s0.2.done: The warped image lines up with the target, and you can explain which matches the RANSAC inlier mask removed.

s07.s0.3.how: Read the CS231n notes on convolutional networks, then work out by hand the output size of a Conv2d layer for a given kernel, stride and padding. Build a small network, print each layer's output shape, and calculate the receptive field of the last layer.
s07.s0.3.done: You predict every layer's output shape before running the model, and the printed shapes match.

s07.s0.4.how: Follow the PyTorch transfer learning tutorial on its ants and bees data. Run it twice: backbone frozen with only the new head trained, then the whole network fine-tuned at a lower learning rate. Record validation accuracy and training time for both.
s07.s0.4.done: You have accuracy and time for both runs and can say when freezing the backbone is the better choice.

s07.s0.5.how: Apply torchvision.transforms.v2 augmentations to a batch and view the results. Find one that changes the label, such as a horizontal flip on left and right arrows or a crop that cuts out the object. For detection, check that the boxes move with the image.
s07.s0.5.done: You can list the augmentations that are safe for your task and one that would corrupt its labels.

s07.s0.6.how: Write an iou(box_a, box_b) function and check it against torchvision.ops.box_iou. Read how mAP averages precision over recall and IoU thresholds, then run validation on a pretrained detector and read its mAP50 and mAP50-95.
s07.s0.6.done: Your IoU matches box_iou on random boxes, and you can explain the difference between mAP50 and mAP50-95.

s07.s0.7.how: Test a trained classifier on images from a different source than its training data: another camera, lighting or background. Compare the accuracy with the original test split, and check that no near-duplicate images sit in both train and test.
s07.s0.7.done: You can report the accuracy drop between the original and the shifted test set and name its likely cause.

s07.s0.8.how: Read frames with cv2.VideoCapture, run a model on each one and measure frames per second. Then process every second or third frame, and batch several frames per forward pass under torch.no_grad(). Compare throughput and latency for each setting.
s07.s0.8.done: You have FPS and per-frame latency for each setting and can say which one meets a stated real-time target.

s07.s1.0.how: Write a short task definition: classes, input images and where the model will run. Collect images or choose a public dataset, split it into train, validation and test folders by source or date so near-duplicates stay in one split, and count images per class.
s07.s1.0.done: You have a written task definition, three split folders, and a per-class count table.

s07.s1.1.how: Train a baseline first: a majority-class predictor and a frozen pretrained backbone with a linear head. Then fine-tune a pretrained torchvision model with augmentation, pick the checkpoint by validation score, and evaluate both on the same test split.
s07.s1.1.done: The fine-tuned model beats the baseline on the test split, and you report the margin.

s07.s1.2.how: Collect test-set predictions and run classification_report for per-class precision, recall and F1, then plot ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions. For a detector, use the per-class mAP table from the validation run instead.
s07.s1.2.done: You can name the two classes the model confuses most, with the count from the confusion matrix.

s07.s1.3.how: Sort test errors by loss or by confidence on the wrong answer, and save the 20 worst to a folder with true and predicted labels in the file names. Tag each with a cause, such as wrong label, blur, occlusion, rare viewpoint or overlapping classes, and count the tags.
s07.s1.3.done: You have a table of error causes with counts and one planned fix for the largest group.

s07.s1.4.how: Write a command with argparse that takes --source as a webcam index, a video file or a folder of images, loads the saved model once, and writes annotated output or a CSV of predictions. Print the average FPS at the end.
s07.s1.4.done: One command runs on all three source types and produces output without any code edits.
